methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective single-institution diagnostic accuracy plus outcomes study of 375 patients, PSM-matched to 163 (101 US vs 62 US+MRI). Strengths: level-by-level pathology-confirmed gold standard, blinded radiologist re-read, PSM with 13 covariates (caliper 0.02, 2:1), standardized outcome definitions (ATA response categories, biochemical complete remission threshold), and Cox regression for RFS. Weaknesses: selection not random (modality chosen by preference), residual confounding remains (authors acknowledge), internal inconsistency in reported sensitivity (abstract: central LN 52.5% -> 90.9%; results: 43.2% -> 91.9%) and LNR figures (results: 0.14 vs 0.24 p<0.001; discussion: 0.31 vs 0.42 p=0.004) suggesting data transcription errors. Subgroup HR=0.24 for CPLN>=2 is reported with inconsistent p-values across sections (p=0.047 log-rank vs p=0.067 multivariable vs p=0.032 abstract).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Retrospective diagnostic accuracy study with outcomes maps to Oxford LoE 3b (individual case-control-like design combined with cohort outcomes). Clinical relevance is direct: reoperative PTC is a difficult surgical scenario where preoperative imaging choice affects dissection strategy. The finding that MRI adjunct substantially improves central compartment LN sensitivity and is associated with higher excellent response rates (50% vs 27.7%) and RFS benefit in CPLN>=2 subgroup has immediate clinical relevance for surgical planning. Findings align with recent 2025 ATA guideline recommendations for cross-sectional imaging when US is inadequate.

reporting_quality.justification: As primarily a diagnostic accuracy study (with outcomes), STARD applies. Key STARD items addressed: index tests (US, MRI) and reference standard (histopathology), flow of participants (Figure 1), imaging criteria for malignancy, blinded re-evaluation, sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV/accuracy reporting, compartment-level analysis, and pre-specified propensity score covariates. Gaps: key numerical inconsistencies between abstract, results, and discussion (sensitivity values and LNR figures) undermine STARD-style transparency; no pre-registration; no confidence intervals for diagnostic metrics in the main text; and the secondary RFS analyses arguably deserve TRIPOD reporting. Data and code are not shared.

novelty_literature.justification: Prior studies (including from the same group, Liu 2014) have demonstrated MRI's value over US for PTC LN detection, and 2025 ATA guidelines already endorse adjunctive cross-sectional imaging. The novel contribution is the linkage from improved imaging detection to surgical quality metrics (LNY, LNR) and oncologic outcomes (biochemical response, RFS in CPLN>=2 subgroup) in the specifically difficult reoperative setting, with a larger cohort than prior series. Meaningful extension rather than a conceptual breakthrough.

writing_presentation.justification: Manuscript is generally clearly written and follows a logical structure. Sections are well labeled; tables and figures are referenced. However, the numerical inconsistencies described above (sensitivity 52.5%/90.9% vs 43.2%/91.9%, LNR 0.14/0.24 vs 0.31/0.42, CPLN HR p-values 0.032 vs 0.047 vs 0.067) significantly reduce clarity. A typo 'USUS-only' appears in the abstract. Some sentences are awkward or redundant. Overall readable but needs careful editing and numerical reconciliation.

key_strengths: Addresses a clinically important and under-studied question in reoperative PTC imaging
Pathology-confirmed level-by-level reference standard with blinded radiologist re-read
Propensity score matching with 13 covariates mitigates some selection bias
Links diagnostic improvement to surgical quality metrics (LNY, LNR) and oncologic outcomes (ATA response, RFS in CPLN>=2 subgroup)
key_concerns: Multiple numerical inconsistencies across abstract/results/discussion (sensitivity, LNR, CPLN HR p-values) raising data-integrity concerns and requiring thorough reconciliation
Selection not random - modality chosen by physician/patient preference - so residual confounding likely remains even after PSM
Typographical error 'USUS-only' in abstract and other minor text problems suggest inadequate proofreading
Subgroup RFS benefit (CPLN>=2) is based on post-hoc exploratory analysis with small subgroup N
No code or data sharing and no confidence intervals for main diagnostic metrics in the main text
chief_reviewer.rationale: Clinically relevant diagnostic-plus-outcomes study undermined by numerical inconsistencies across sections and unclear reconciliation. Fits Tier 3 with major revisions to correct numerical errors and clarify statistical reporting.
